item.statement_excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $E\to\overline{\mathbb D}$ be a smooth complex vector bundle of rank $m\ge1$, with complex multiplication $J$, and let $F\subset E|_{\partial\mathbb D}$ be a smooth oriented totally real real subbundle of rank $m$. Let $P$ be a smooth real-linear first-order operator on sections with exact Cauchy–Riemann symbol: for real smooth $h$ and smooth $\xi$,
$$P(h\xi)=hP\xi+h_x\xi+h_yJ\xi.$$
Use smooth positive definite metrics and finite smooth charts to define $H^r(E)$ by weak derivatives for integers $r\ge1$. Let $X_0$ be the $H^1$ closure of smooth sections with boundary values in $F$, and put $X_q=H^{q+1}(E)\cap X_0$, $Y_q=H^q(E)$ for integers $q\ge0$. Only the zeroth boundary condition is imposed.

There is a smooth global complex frame of $E$ and an integer $k$ in which the boundary condition is
$$F(e^{it})=e^{ikt}\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R^{m-1}$$
and the actual operator is $\partial_x+i\partial_y+B$ with smooth real-linear zeroth-order coefficient $B$. Equivalently, before this reduction, if $C(t)$ is the complex matrix whose columns are any smooth periodic oriented real frame of $F$ in any global complex frame, then
$$k=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{(\det C)'(t)}{\det C(t)}\,dt.$$
Such frames exist, and this integer is independent of both choices.

Every actual realization $P_q:X_q\to Y_q$ is bounded Fredholm with real index $m+2k$. Its kernel is the same set as the $H^1$ kernel, its range is $Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0$, and inclusion in $L^2$ identifies its real cokernel with that of $P_0$. For $\xi\in X_0$ and $P\xi=f\in H^q$,
$$\|\xi\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|\xi\|_{H^1}).$$
The inverse of $P_0$ from its $H^1$ kernel complement to its closed range is bounded, and its restriction gives a bounded range inverse $H^q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0\to X_q$. The statement applies to an actual geometric linearization along a smooth disk with oriented totally real boundary. It does not assert its surjectivity, compute a Heegaard domain formula, or supply a puncture or gluing theorem.

proof_step_donor_fragments.exact_current_text: Construct a genuine smooth global complex frame. A finite complex bundle atlas and smooth finite partition give a complex embedding $e_z:E_z\to\mathbb C^N$, for instance $e_z(v)=(\phi_i(z)\tau_i(v))_i$ in local frames; each term is supported inside its chart and at least one $\phi_i$ is nonzero. Its image has smooth Hermitian orthogonal projection $Q(z)=e_z(e_z^*e_z)^{-1}e_z^*$, using any fixed smooth Hermitian metric on $E$. Such a metric is the finite positive partition sum of the local ones. Along each radius $z\mapsto\lambda z$, $0\le\lambda\le1$, set $K=[\partial_\lambda Q,Q]$. It is a smooth complex skew-Hermitian matrix, and solve $W_\lambda=KW$, $W(0,z)=I$, by its iterated-integral series. On this compact parameter set the term of length $n$ is bounded by $M^n/n!$; every fixed number of $z$ derivatives adds only a polynomial in $n$ times finitely many coefficient bounds, so the series is smooth jointly, including at $z=0$. Its integral equation gives the stated ODE, and uniqueness follows by iterating the difference integral bound and letting $n\to\infty$. Since $Q^2=Q$, differentiation gives $[K,Q]=\partial_\lambda Q$. Thus $(W^{-1}Q(\lambda z)W)_\lambda=0$. Also $(W^*W)_\lambda=0$, so $W$ is unitary and maps $\operatorname{Ran}Q(0)$ to $\operatorname{Ran}Q(z)$ at $\lambda=1$. Transport any one complex basis at zero and apply $e_z^{-1}$. This yields a smooth global frame, with all derivatives bounded on the closed disk. Only finite-dimensional operations and specified convergent series were used. [given, construct, algebra]

In that frame regard $F(t)$ as a smooth oriented real subspace of $\mathbb C^m$. Its real orthogonal projection is smooth. The same projection-commutator ODE, now along $0\le t\le2\pi$ with real matrices, transports one oriented orthonormal real basis of $F(0)$ to a smooth basis $b(t)$. Because the projection is periodic, continuation satisfies $b(t+2\pi)=b(t)A$ for an orthogonal matrix $A$; its determinant is positive, since the transported frame preserves its agreement sign with the given orientation of $F$. Thus $A\in SO(m)$. There is a smooth path in $SO(m)$ from $I$ to $A^{-1}$, stationary near its ends: successively rotate a unit first column to the first coordinate vector in real coordinate two-planes, then do the same in the remaining orthogonal block, and finish with the determinant-one last coordinate; finitely many plane rotations supply such a path, each angle reparametrized by a smooth step. For $m=1$, $A=1$. Multiply $b(t)$ on the right by that path, chosen constant $I$ near zero and $A^{-1}$ near $2\pi$. The new frame is periodic with every derivative, because near the terminal endpoint it is exactly $b(t)A^{-1}=b(t-2\pi)$. Its columns form a smooth periodic oriented real frame of $F$. They are also complex independent by total reality, so their matrix $C(t)$ lies in $GL_m(\mathbb C)$. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Let $k$ be the determinant winding of $C$. It is an integer by [F1]. The loop $G(t)=C(t)\operatorname{diag}(e^{-ikt},1,\ldots,1)$ has zero determinant winding, so [F1] extends it to a smooth invertible complex matrix $\widehat G$ on the disk. Change the global complex frame by $\widehat G$. On its boundary the new coordinates of $F$ are exactly $\operatorname{diag}(e^{ikt},1,\ldots,1)\mathbb R^m$. A change of periodic oriented real boundary basis multiplies $C$ by a loop in $GL_m^+(\mathbb R)$, whose positive real determinant has winding zero. A change of global complex frame multiplies it by the inverse boundary value of a disk matrix; that determinant also has winding zero by [F1]. Additivity therefore proves independence of $k$. In the new frame the symbol is exactly $\partial_x+i\partial_y$, and subtracting that symbol leaves a smooth real-linear multiplication coefficient $B$: an operator of order at most one with zero first-order symbol is zeroth order in local coordinates. This proves the claimed actual normal form. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Frame multiplication and its inverse are bounded on every integer Sobolev space by repeated Leibniz, since the coefficient matrices and all their derivatives are bounded on the compact disk. They identify smooth boundary-compatible sections with smooth maps in the canonical boundary planes. Consequently they identify their $H^1$ completions. By [F2] this canonical completion is exactly $X_{2k}\oplus X_0^{m-1}$ in its scalar notation, not an unproved larger weak-trace domain. They also identify each indicated higher space as its $H^{q+1}$ intersection with that same closed $H^1$ condition, imposing no higher trace. The metrics give equivalent norms because their positive eigenvalues have a positive compact minimum. Thus every following operator and norm assertion transfers to the original geometric bundle. [F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

The unperturbed canonical operator $T=\partial_x+i\partial_y$ is the direct sum of the scalar operators with parameters $2k,0,\ldots,0$ from [F2]. It is Fredholm of real index $(2k+1)+(m-1)=m+2k$. It has actual finite-error parametrices on both sides. To see this from the stated scalar formulas, let $B_0$ be their finite-dimensional obstruction map and $R_0$ its explicit bounded right inverse on its finite-dimensional target, and let $Q_0$ be their bounded inverse on the range. Then $S=Q_0(I-R_0B_0)$ is bounded on the whole target and $TS=I-R_0B_0$. Also $ST=Q_0T$; hence $I-ST$ has image in the finite-dimensional kernel of $T$, because applying $T$ gives zero. These identities work componentwise when the obstruction target or kernel is zero. [F2, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

We establish the missing local weak higher regularity at the boundary. A holomorphic source coordinate straightens the disk circle near any one boundary point: after rotation one may use $w=i(1-z)/(1+z)$, avoiding its pole. Its derivative is nonzero on a smaller neighborhood. The operator transforms to a nonzero smooth complex scalar times $D_0$ plus a smooth zeroth-order matrix; divide that scalar. On this local boundary interval the canonical target real frame $\operatorname{diag}(e^{ikt},1,\ldots,1)$ has a smooth complex extension across a collar, obtained by extending the local smooth argument coordinate. Multiplying by that extension makes the local boundary condition the constant $\mathbb R^m$, and the operator is $D_0+C$ with smooth $C$. Interior patches need no boundary gauge. For a compactly supported smooth halfplane section real on the straight edge, integration by parts gives $\|D_0v\|_2^2=\|v_x\|_2^2+\|v_y\|_2^2$: the interior mixed terms cancel, and the edge term has zero real part because $v,v_x$ are real there. The estimate passes to its $H^1$ boundary completion. Real even/imaginary odd reflection followed by symmetric convolution proves the relevant local approximation, since values match at the seam and integration by parts verifies the weak $H^1$ extension; this is only an $H^1$ assertion. Interior compact patches use the same full-plane identity. Adding $\|v\|_2$ gives the local $H^1$ estimate for $D_0+C$. [step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Multiplication by $B$ is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank maps $H^1(\mathbb D)\to L^2(\mathbb D)$; here is the compactness proof needed, without an imported Rellich theorem. For smooth $v$ extend it outside the disk by $Ev(re^{it})=\chi(r)v((2-r)e^{it})$ for $1<r<4/3$, where $\chi=1$ near one and vanishes near $4/3$, and set it zero beyond. Inside the disk set $Ev=v$. The values match at $r=1$, so integration by parts across that circle cancels the boundary terms and gives the piecewise derivatives as global weak derivatives. On this annulus $2-r\in[2/3,1]$; polar area and derivative factors have bounded ratios. Thus $\|Ev\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^2)}\le C\|v\|_{H^1(\mathbb D)}$. Extend this map to the disk completion. Partition a fixed enclosing square into cells of side $h$ and replace $Ev$ on each cell by its average. Coordinate-segment fundamental theorems and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|Ev-\operatorname{av}_h Ev\|_2\le Ch\|\nabla Ev\|_2$: subtract the cell average, use the double-integral variance identity, and join two points by first a horizontal and then a vertical segment; integrating the unused coordinates yields the factor $h^2$ in the squared estimate. The estimate passes to weak $H^1$ functions by plane convolution, whose function and weak derivative convergence follows from $L^2$ translation continuity. Restricting the cell averages to the disk gives a finite-rank $J_h$ with $\|v-J_hv\|_2\le Ch\|v\|_{H^1}$. Therefore $BJ_h$ converges in norm to multiplication by the bounded matrix $B$. Restricting to the closed boundary domain retains finite rank and that estimate. Apply [F3] to the finite-error parametrix in step 5.1 and this perturbation. It gives actual Fredholmness of $P_0=T+B$, index $m+2k$, closed range and its bounded inverse on the $H^1$ kernel complement. [F3, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

Let $(D_0+C)v=g\in H^1$ on a local patch with its actual $H^1$ boundary condition. Use nested cutoffs to work with compact support, preserving that real condition. Longitudinal difference quotients in the straight tangential coordinate preserve it. Their equation has forcing $\delta_hg-C_h\delta_hv-(\delta_hC)v$, plus the cutoff terms. The $L^2$ norm of $\delta_hv$ is bounded by the $L^2$ tangential derivative of $v$; $\delta_hg$ is bounded by that of $g$. The smooth first coefficient derivatives and step 5.2 therefore bound these difference quotients in $H^1$ on a smaller patch. The bounded-test Hilbert representation argument [F4] gives $v_x\in H^1$ there, in the same weakly closed real boundary domain. The equation $v_y=-i(g-Cv-v_x)$ then puts $v_y$ in $H^1$. This proves $H^2$ and its local estimate. For the induction, once $v\in H^q$, the tangential derivative solves $(D_0+C)v_x=g_x-C_xv\in H^{q-1}$ and still has the real $H^1$ condition. Apply the already proved order-$q-1$ estimate on nested smaller patches; it gives $v_x\in H^q$, then the equation gives $v_y\in H^q$. Thus $v\in H^{q+1}$ with a bound by $\|g\|_{H^q}$ and the original $H^1$ norm. All cutoff derivatives contribute only controlled lower-order terms. A finite patch cover, the smooth source and target transformations, and compact partitions yield the stated global estimate. This proves regularity for the actual weak disk domain rather than assuming differentiated normal boundary conditions. [F4, step 5.2, construct, algebra]

The weak Sobolev spaces are Hilbert: their finite weak-derivative graphs are closed in the finite $L^2$ sum, by passing the test identities to norm limits. The higher domains are closed Hilbert subspaces of $H^{q+1}$ because their $H^1$ condition is closed, and the operator is bounded there. Step 6.2 gives $\ker P_q=\ker P_0$ and $\operatorname{Ran}P_q=H^q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0$. This range is closed in $H^q$. The quotient map $H^q\to L^2/\operatorname{Ran}P_0$ is onto: smooth compactly supported interior sections are dense in $L^2$ by local cutoff and convolution and belong to $H^q$; their image is dense in that finite-dimensional quotient, while every linear subspace of a finite-dimensional space is closed. Its kernel is exactly the higher range. Thus both kernel and cokernel dimensions agree, and the actual index remains $m+2k$. Finally restrict the bounded $H^1$ range inverse from step 6.1; step 6.2 puts its higher forcing solutions in $H^{q+1}$ with bounded norm, as asserted. All infinite constructions were finite-rank norm approximations, specified matrix-ODE series or the Countable-Choice Hilbert procedures in the cited proved suppliers. The theorem supplies actual geometric disk Fredholm theory, not surjectivity, Heegaard-domain index identification, puncture matching or nonlinear gluing. [F3, F4, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 6.2, construct, algebra] ∎
